### Observed differences

- **Resource allocation changed for six activities (A01, A03, A13, A14, A17, A21).** In the earlier window, each of these activities was led by a group of resources holding roughly 4–10 in 100 assignments apiece; in the later window, the leading shares belong to a largely different group: User_78 becomes the top assignee for all six activities (about 8–12 in 100, from unlisted before), User_12 holds about 5–6 in 100 and User_77 about 4–7 in 100, while most previously frequent resources fall to low shares or drop out of the leading group entirely. One resource keeps a similar mid-level share (about 5–8 in 100) in both windows, and the residual "other" share grows slightly (for A01, from about 49 to 55 in 100). The profiles rest on roughly 130–300 assignment observations per window, the fewest for A21. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]

- **Timing.** The elapsed time between consecutive completion events for A04 and A01 roughly doubled: the mean rose from about 29 h to about 56 h, the median from about 22 h to about 45 h, and the upper quartile from about 33 h to about 72 h, while the lowest quarter of intervals stayed near zero in both windows (200 intervals per window). [TWAIT001]

- **Screening context.** The resource family produced 6 qualifying items against about 0.005 expected without change, the time family 1 item against about 0.017, and the control-flow family 0 items against about 0.17 — so the resource differences far exceed what random re-splits produce, and no structural or routing difference qualified at the configured thresholds. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, TWAIT001]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports a reallocation of work: for activities A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A21, execution shifted from one group of resources to a largely different group — in the later window User_78, User_12 and User_77 took over the leading shares, while a largely disjoint set of previously frequent resources stopped receiving work, with one resource keeping a similar share throughout. This rests on six allocation profiles that all moved in the same direction with the same gainers, on a resource-family count (6) many times its chance expectation (about 0.005), and on per-item differences larger than in about 999.5 of 1000 random re-splits. Limitations: the items are not fully independent — A13 and A14 show identical profiles, and all six may express one global reallocation rather than six separate per-activity changes; the resource codes are anonymous, so no roles or teams can be inferred. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]

Other differences: the interval between consecutive completions of A04 and A01 roughly doubled (median about 22 h to about 45 h). As the only time item (1 against about 0.017 expected in its family), it does not by itself rule out a sampling fluke, and it is not part of the allocation hypothesis. [TWAIT001]

An important competing explanation the evidence cannot rule out: the shift could reflect a changed resource pool (resources entering or leaving) rather than reassignment of work within the same pool — both would produce the same allocation profiles. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
